title: Binary Search Trees
summary: A binary tree with an ordering rule that turns search into a sequence of simple choices.
keyPoints: Every value in the left subtree is smaller than the node, and every value in the right subtree is larger.
Search follows one branch per level, so it costs O(h) where h is the height.
A balanced BST has height O(log n); a skewed BST has height O(n).
Inorder traversal of a valid BST produces sorted order.

complexity.note: Balanced h = log n; skewed h = n.
Sorted order for a valid BST.

commonMistakes: Checking only the immediate children instead of the allowed range for the whole subtree.
Assuming a BST is balanced; insertion order can make it a linked list.
Deleting a node with two children without finding a replacement from one subtree.
Using inorder traversal to verify a BST when a range check is simpler and avoids extra memory.
interviewNotes: If the tree is a BST, mention that search can prune an entire subtree at each step.
For validation, carry low and high bounds down the recursion; comparing with the parent alone is not enough.
For kth smallest, either do an inorder walk or store subtree sizes if the tree supports rank queries.

checkYourself.question: Why is comparing a node only with its parent insufficient for validation?
checkYourself.answer: A value deep in the left subtree can still be larger than an ancestor even if it is smaller than its local parent. The whole allowed range must be checked.

checkYourself.question: What is the height of a BST built from sorted ascending input?
checkYourself.answer: n - 1, because every new value becomes the right child of the previous node. The tree is skewed.

checkYourself.question: How do you find the kth smallest value?
checkYourself.answer: Walk inorder and count visits, stopping at k. Or use subtree sizes to skip whole left subtrees.
